title: High-Throughput Structure Prediction with BioNeMo Inference Runtime | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA's BioNeMo Inference Runtime (BioIR) claims a 2.90x improvement in residue-normalized folding throughput over a torch-compiled open-source Boltz-2 on 8xH100 (58.5K vs 20.2K residues per GPU-hour), plus a roughly 3x reduction in estimated folding energy (11 MWh vs 35 MWh per million targets). The proof point is production scale, not a demo: BioIR-derived modules powered the AlphaFold Database expansion across 4,777 proteomes and about 31 million candidate complexes, of which 1.81 million were released as high-confidence predictions.

insights.claim: In a matched benchmark of 1,000 human dimer targets on 8xH100 GPUs, the NVIDIA-accelerated Boltz-2 runtime delivered 58.5K successfully folded residues per allocated GPU-hour versus 20.2K for a torch-compiled open-source implementation — a 2.90x improvement in residue-normalized throughput.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Structure-prediction compute cost per target can drop ~3x on identical hardware, shifting the bottleneck in AI drug discovery from GPU budget back to wet-lab validation and data.
insights.quote: BioIR completed all 1,000 targets and delivered 58.5K successfully folded residues per allocated GPU-hour, compared with 20.2K for the public implementation—a 2.90× improvement in residue-normalized throughput
insights.locator: Step 6. Benchmark folding-stage efficiency

insights.claim: The open-source baseline implementation ran out of memory on 29 of 1,000 targets while the accelerated runtime completed all of them, making reliability — not just speed — part of the measured gap.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: A ~3% failure rate on open-source tooling compounds badly at proteome scale; completion rate is an underrated cost driver in high-throughput pipelines.
insights.quote: the open-source implementation ran out of memory on 29 targets
insights.locator: Step 6. Benchmark folding-stage efficiency

insights.claim: Biomolecular structure prediction is characterized as now routinely running at proteome scale, where the operational goal is moving an entire worklist through a pipeline efficiently rather than predicting single structures.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: The buying unit in computational biology is shifting from per-prediction accuracy to throughput-per-dollar, which favors vendors selling pipeline infrastructure over model quality alone.
insights.quote: Biomolecular structure prediction is now often run at proteome scale, where the goal is to move an entire worklist through the pipeline efficiently.
insights.locator: Biomolecular structure prediction is now often run

insights.claim: The benchmark workflow used a demanding inference recipe — three recycles, 200 sampling steps and five diffusion samples per target — on dimers under 2,800 combined residues, so the quoted throughput reflects high-quality settings rather than a cheap configuration.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Comparable numbers require matching recycle and diffusion-sample counts; without them, folding-throughput claims across vendors are not comparable.
insights.quote: The workflow used three recycles, 200 sampling steps, and five diffusion samples per target.
insights.locator: Step 6. Benchmark folding-stage efficiency

themes.theme: Energy as the emerging cost metric

insights.claim: Extrapolated linearly to one million comparable targets, the accelerated runtime is estimated to consume 11 MWh versus 35 MWh for the public implementation using 8-GPU TDP equivalents, and 21 MWh versus 64 MWh using full-node maximum-power equivalents.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Software efficiency is now marketed in megawatt-hours — the clearest sign that power, not GPU supply, is becoming the binding constraint buyers price.
insights.quote: BioIR is estimated to require 11 MWh versus 35 MWh for the public implementation using 8-GPU TDP (Thermal Design Power) equivalents, and 21 MWh versus 64 MWh using full-node maximum-power equivalents.
insights.locator: We linearly extrapolated the 1000-target matched benchmark

insights.claim: The energy figures are explicitly labeled as folding-only rated-power estimates for IT equipment, excluding metered measurement and data center overhead such as power usage effectiveness.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Real facility energy would be materially higher once PUE is applied; treat vendor MWh claims as lower bounds when modeling datacenter power demand.
insights.quote: These are folding-only estimates for IT equipment, not metered energy measurements, and exclude data center overhead, such as power usage effectiveness (PUE).
insights.locator: We linearly extrapolated the 1000-target matched benchmark

insights.claim: The runtime separates optimization into three distinct layers — kernel selection, module optimization via CUDA Graph capture, and pipeline scaling through Ray replicas — each attacking a different bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: A transferable mental model for evaluating any inference-acceleration claim: ask which layer the speedup came from, because only kernel and module gains survive hardware or workload changes.
insights.quote: Kernel and module optimizations reduce model-forward time within a replica.
insights.locator: Step 5. Separate per-replica acceleration from pipeline scaling

insights.claim: Kernel selection is dynamic — supported operations pick among custom, cuEquivariance, or PyTorch fallback implementations based on model configuration, GPU, data type and tensor shape at runtime.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Per-shape, per-GPU kernel dispatch is expensive engineering that open-source projects rarely sustain — this is the durable part of the moat, not the headline multiple.
insights.quote: Supported operations select compatible BioIR custom, cuEquivariance, or PyTorch fallback implementations based on the model configuration, GPU, data type, and tensor shape.
insights.locator: Kernel selection:

insights.claim: The Ray executor scales throughput only by running complete model replicas on separate GPUs for independent inputs; it explicitly does not split a single model forward pass across GPUs.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Latency on any single large target is capped by one GPU's memory and speed, so this architecture scales batch screening but not individual hard targets — a real limit for time-critical workflows.
insights.quote: Ray does not split a single model forward pass across GPUs.
insights.locator: Step 5. Separate per-replica acceleration from pipeline scaling

insights.claim: Because every Ray actor loads the full model and reserves one GPU, the capacity rule engine compute multiplied by num_gpus must not exceed visible GPUs — memory per GPU, not aggregate cluster memory, sets the replica ceiling.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Scaling this pipeline means buying more GPUs with adequate individual HBM rather than pooling memory, keeping demand pointed at high-memory parts.
insights.quote: The capacity rule is engine_stage.compute × engine_stage.num_gpus ≤ visible GPUs.
insights.locator: Step 3. Scale independent inputs with Ray replicas

insights.claim: Whether overlapping CPU stages with GPU inference actually helps depends on the runtime cost of parsing, feature generation and output writing for a given input and hardware configuration, so pipeline parallelism is not a universal win.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: CPU preprocessing can silently become the bottleneck in GPU pipelines — a reason total system cost per structure diverges from GPU-hour cost.
insights.quote: Ray is designed to overlap CPU stages with inference, but whether this improves the target workload depends on the run time cost of the parsing, feature generation, and output writing stages
insights.locator: Step 4. Balance the five processor stages

themes.theme: Production proof point at AlphaFold Database scale

insights.claim: The runtime was used in the recent expansion of the AlphaFold Database, generating protein-complex structures across 4,777 proteomes and roughly 31 million candidate complexes, of which 1.81 million were released as high-confidence predictions.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: A roughly 6% high-confidence yield from 31 million candidates shows how much compute is spent on predictions that get discarded — throughput economics, not accuracy, gate this kind of science.
insights.quote: accelerating the generation of protein-complex structures across 4,777 proteomes, about 31 million candidate complexes in total, with 1.81 million released as high-confidence predictions
insights.locator: BioIR has also been used in real proteome-scale work

insights.claim: An early version of the runtime contributed accelerated modules to an NVIDIA-internal version of OpenFold2-MM, which is what enabled the 31-million-complex AlphaFold Database run — meaning a public scientific resource was produced on proprietary, internal-only accelerated code.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Foundational open biology datasets are increasingly dependent on one vendor's private optimization stack, a quiet form of infrastructure dependency worth tracking.
insights.quote: An early version of BIR contributed accelerated modules to an NVIDIA-internal version of OpenFold2-MM, which enabled protein structure predictions at scale for the AFDB with 31 million protein complex structures.
insights.locator: Similar to Boltz2 accelerations

insights.claim: The acceleration work extends beyond one model to other biomolecular cofolding models including OpenFold2 and OpenFold3, indicating a platform strategy rather than a single-model optimization.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: If the runtime becomes the default execution layer for every major cofolding model, model differentiation shifts upstream and the infrastructure layer captures the value.
insights.locator: Similar to Boltz2 accelerations

themes.theme: Adoption friction removed and ecosystem capture

insights.claim: The distributed wheel contains precompiled CUBINs, so runtime use requires no nvcc, CUDA source, CMake or CUDA toolkit installation.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Removing the compiler-toolchain barrier lets biologists rather than HPC engineers adopt GPU acceleration — the classic mechanism by which CUDA's installed base widens.
insights.quote: The wheel contains precompiled CUBINs, so runtime use does not require nvcc, CUDA source, CMake, or the CUDA toolkit.
insights.locator: Prerequisites

insights.claim: The runtime is deliberately offered both as an end-to-end processor and as directly importable torch.nn.Module components, preserving the familiar PyTorch workflow instead of forcing a proprietary serving framework.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Meeting researchers inside PyTorch lowers switching cost to near zero going in and raises it going out — lock-in through convenience rather than through a closed platform.
insights.quote: Direct PyTorch integration lets you construct a supported model (torch.nn.Module) or reuse selected modules in custom code.
insights.locator: You can use it in two ways

insights.claim: The runtime deliberately omits MSA search — it does not run HHsearch or HMMsearch and requires a pre-staged A3M multiple sequence alignment for every protein chain.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: MSA generation remains an unaccelerated CPU-bound cost outside the quoted speedups, leaving an open niche for whoever solves that stage.
insights.quote: You can optionally supply templates yourself because BioIR does not run HHsearch or HMMsearch.
insights.locator: Step 1. Choose a supported structure-prediction workflow

insights.claim: The end-to-end processor supports ligand structure prediction but explicitly not ligand-affinity prediction, leaving the binding-strength step that pharma cares most about outside the accelerated path.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: The commercially decisive affinity-prediction step is still a gap, which bounds how much of the drug-discovery pipeline this tooling currently owns.
insights.quote: The end-to-end processor supports ligand structure prediction, but not ligand-affinity prediction.
insights.locator: Step 1. Choose a supported structure-prediction workflow

insights.claim: Users are pointed onward to the BioNeMo Agent Toolkit for agentic orchestration of drug discovery workflows, signaling that the runtime is one layer of a broader agent-driven discovery stack.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Watch for the value to migrate up to agentic orchestration of discovery campaigns, where the vendor can attach to scientific decision-making rather than just compute.
insights.locator: Get started

insights.claim: The controlled comparison explicitly excludes MSA generation, preprocessing CPU allocations, storage, data transfer, retries and engineering overhead, so the 2.90x figure covers only the folding stage.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Real end-to-end pipeline speedup will be lower than the advertised multiple; underwrite total cost per delivered structure, not per folding forward pass.
insights.quote: it excludes MSA generation, preprocessing CPU allocations, storage, data transfer, retries, and engineering overhead
insights.locator: The controlled comparison measures folding throughput

insights.claim: Model-forward speedup figures were measured with a single warmup and a single measurement call across only 17 inputs spanning 29 to 1,734 residues, a small sample that the author presents as early benchmarking.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: The geometric-mean kernel speedups rest on a thin sample; only the 1,000-target end-to-end benchmark carries real statistical weight.
insights.quote: Speedups measured using 1 warmup run (discarded) and 1 measurement call across 17 inputs spanning 29–1,734 residues.
insights.locator: Our early benchmarking with BioNeMo Inference Runtime

insights.claim: The author insists model-forward latency and end-to-end pipeline metrics must be reported separately, and warns against repeating one input row as evidence of useful scaling.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: A concrete anti-pattern checklist for auditing AI infrastructure benchmarks: duplicated inputs and conflated metrics are the two most common ways speedups get inflated.
insights.quote: do not repeat one row as evidence of useful scaling
insights.locator: Replace the truncated sequence and MSA path

insights.claim: The recommended set of end-to-end metrics is completed structures per hour, GPU and CPU utilization, peak GPU memory, completion rate, failures and retries — a broader scorecard than raw throughput.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Use completion rate and retries alongside throughput when comparing AI infrastructure vendors; failure rates are where advertised savings often disappear.
insights.quote: including completed structures per hour, GPU and CPU utilization, peak GPU memory, completion rate, failures, and retries
insights.locator: The controlled comparison measures folding throughput

insights.claim: The vendor warns that throughput metrics are specific to the tested configuration and should not be generalized to other supported models, datasets or hardware.
insights.speaker: Kyle Tretina
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate the 2.90x across a model portfolio; each model-hardware pair needs its own measurement before budgeting savings.
insights.quote: throughput metrics and other results are specific to this configuration and should not be generalized to all BioIR-supported models, datasets, or hardware
